entities.name: Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum, opened 1996 in Nagasaki, Japan (replacing a smaller exhibition hall), documents the August 9, 1945 plutonium implosion bomb 'Fat Man' (21 kiloton yield) that killed 35,000-40,000 people instantly and 60,000-80,000 total in a city that was not the primary target that day (Kokura was, but cloud cover redirected the mission to Nagasaki) — making it a memorial to both the second nuclear attack and the contingency by which a city became the world's last nuclear victim. The museum complements Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Museum in Japan's nuclear testimony.

'Fat Man' exploded at 11:02 AM on August 9, 1945, 503 meters above Nagasaki's Urakami district — 2.5 km north of the intended aim point due to cloud cover. The hypocenter was the Urakami Cathedral district, home to Nagasaki's large Catholic community: the cathedral (rebuilt 1925) was destroyed. Nagasaki had been Japan's only open port for European trade from 1641-1853 (Dutch East India Company trading post on Dejima island) — the bombing destroyed a city with the longest continuous Western contact history in Japan.

The Nagasaki museum's exhibits include a melted rosary (fused by the bomb's heat), the reconstructed iron cross from Urakami Cathedral, deformed bottles and tiles, and the famous photograph of the 'Nagasaki boy' (Tanimoto's photograph of a standing boy cremating his younger brother in post-bomb Nagasaki) that became iconic. The museum opened in 1996 — 51 years after the bombing — as part of Japan's commitment to nuclear testimony ahead of the NPT Review Conference.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum documents not only the second nuclear attack but its contingency — the cloud cover over Kokura that redirected the mission — making it a memorial to how random targeting decisions killed a city of Catholic Christians who had maintained Japan's longest Western contact, a confluence of ironies unique in military history.
